newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary FinMin - economy improving, but not enough.
newsitem.headline: Hungary FinMin - economy improving, but not enough.

text.p: Hungary has reduced its foreign debt and current account deficit and lowered inflation, but the economy's overall performance in 1996 was not satisfactory, Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy said on Friday.

"I'm not really satisfied with the overall performance of the economy, although I understand why it was not as strong as we would have liked it to be, but our indicators are very favourable on the area of balance," he told a news conference.
Last year's policies aimed to continue the stabilisation programme launched by former finance minister Lajos Bokros in March 1995, Medgyessy said.
"The performance of the economy reflects the adjustment phase the Hungarian economy has experienced recently," he said.
The Finance Ministry estimates gross domestic product (GDP) was flat in 1996 and forecasts two percent growth in 1997.
But industrial output showed about three percent real growth in 1996, a revival concentrated in the last months of the year, Medgyessy said.

Investment was very weak in first-half 1996, showed some improvement in the third quarter, but still fell 7.5 percent in January-September from the same 1995 period, he said. Full 1996 investment was expected to be unchanged from 1995, he added.
The foreign trade deficit is seen around $2.5 billion, based on exports totalling $16 to $16.5 billion and imports of $18.5 to $18.7 billion, he said.
The current account deficit is seen amounting to some $1.5 billion in 1996, below the planned $2 billion deficit and below the 1995 deficit of $2.5 billion.
"Capital inflow is continuing with the size of inflow substantially surpassing the current account deficit," Medgyessy said.
Hungary's foreign debt also fell last year, he said. The net debt in 1996 was roughly equal to the year's exports, while in 1994 the debt was 1.8 times that year's exports, he said.
The central budget is expected to end the year with a deficit of 130 billion forints, well below the 233 billion forint target set in the budget law.

Hungary trimmed inflation to 19.8 percent year-on-year in December, from 29.2 percent last January. "This is still extraordinarily high," he said, adding that average inflation for 1996 would be somewhat above 23 percent.
"To reduce inflation by around an annual five percent is a realistic target," Medgyessy said.
